property_summary: After any single successful airDrop call by an address A, the contract remains unlocked allowing a subsequent airDrop by a different address B to increase B's tokenBalance by 20; the mutant that never clears the reentrancy lock breaks this because once any caller uses airDrop the contract stays locked and further airDrop calls revert or have no effect for some B.

For any caller address A, after calling airDrop from A the reference contract C only ever increases tokenBalance at A (i.e., no call can change tokenBalance for any other key); the mutant removing hasNoBalance allows calls that change balances for keys other than the caller (because callers with existing balances can be treated differently), so there exist inputs where tokenBalance(k) differs between P and M.

For every caller address a, the reference C only allows airDrop to increase tokenBalance(a) when the caller had zero prior balance (hasNoBalance), so after any airDrop call tokenBalance for addresses other than the caller remains unchanged; the mutant (which removed hasNoBalance) permits airDrop from callers with non-zero balances and can cause tokenBalance at some key k to differ from the reference.

In the reference, any call to airDrop can only ever increase tokenBalance at the caller's address and leaves all other addresses' balances unchanged; the mutant (removing hasNoBalance) allows a call to airDrop that can change tokenBalance at some OTHER address for some caller, so there exists a fuzzed caller/attacker address that causes tokenBalance(k) to differ for some k after the call.

For every caller address a and any target address k, calling airDrop from a on the correct contract never changes tokenBalance(k) when k != a (only caller's own balance may increase and only if it was zero); the mutant removing the hasNoBalance modifier allows calls that can change balances for other keys, so there exist inputs (caller, target k) where tokenBalance(k) differs after airDrop.

For every caller address a and any address k, if k != a then a call to airDrop from a on the reference contract never changes tokenBalance(k); the mutant (which removed hasNoBalance) can cause some other address's tokenBalance(k) to change for some caller a and some k, so there exist fuzzed addresses that make tokenBalance(k) differ after airDrop.

For any caller address, when they call airDrop the reference contract always increases their tokenBalance by 20 (from 0 to 20 because hasNoBalance requires zero) — the mutant that compares to the wrong string prevents the supportsToken check from passing for a legitimate Bank contract and therefore can make airDrop not execute, breaking the rule for some caller.

For any caller address A that initially has zero tokenBalance, after A calls airDrop through a supporting Bank, reference C always grants A +20 tokens (tokenBalance[A] == 20) while the mutant that inverts hasNoBalance can block such new callers so there exist inputs where tokenBalance differs.

For any caller who already holds a positive token balance, calling airDrop increments their balance by 20; the mutant that inverted hasNoBalance blocks callers with zero balance and thus can make balances differ for some callers.

For any caller address that currently has zero tokenBalance and that is a Bank supporting the token, calling airDrop will result in that caller having tokenBalance == 20 in the correct contract; the mutant inverting hasNoBalance blocks zero-balance callers and thus violates this by leaving some callers at 0.

For any caller address, after a single call to airDrop the caller's tokenBalance is increased by exactly 20 (no more) because the reference uses a reentrancy lock; the mutant that fails to set the lock allows a reentrant attacker to receive >20 (violating the rule) for some attacker-driven input.

For any caller address and any initial balance, a single call to airDrop increases that caller's tokenBalance by exactly 20 (reference enforces this via a reentrancy guard); the mutant removing the guard allows a reentrant attacker to obtain >20 in some input, violating the rule.

For any caller address, after a single call to airDrop by that address, the caller's tokenBalance increases by at most 20 in the correct contract (reentrancy guard prevents recursive gains); the mutant that removes setting _locked = true enables reentrancy allowing some attacker contracts to end up with tokenBalance > 20.

For every caller that is a contract which reports support for the token string, a single external call to airDrop must leave that caller's tokenBalance equal to exactly 20 in the correct contract; the mutant that fails to set the reentrancy lock allows a malicious callee (which re-enters during supportsToken) to cause the final tokenBalance to be greater than 20 for some fuzzed attacker address, violating the rule.

For every caller contract that advertises support (supportsToken), a single call to airDrop() on the correct contract always results in the call succeeding (does not revert) because the reentrancy guard prevents recursive re-entry during supportsToken; the mutant that corrupts the guard can allow a reentrant attacker to cause airDrop to revert for some attacker implementation, breaking the rule.

For any caller address with zero prior tokenBalance, calling airDrop always increases their tokenBalance by exactly 20 in the reference; the mutant that adds 40 will sometimes make the resulting tokenBalance != 20, so the rule (balance == 20 after airDrop) is violated for some fuzzed caller addresses.

For any caller with zero prior tokenBalance, calling airDrop results in tokenBalance == 20 in the reference implementation; the mutant that adds 40 will produce tokenBalance != 20 for some caller (breaking the rule).

For any caller address that currently has zero tokenBalance and whose msg.sender (as a contract) reports support for the token, calling airDrop increases their tokenBalance by exactly 20 in the reference; the mutant that adds 40 will make the final tokenBalance != 20 for some admissible caller contract address.

For any caller that is a contract which advertises support for the token and currently has zero tokenBalance, after calling airDrop the reference contract always increases that caller's tokenBalance by exactly 20; the mutant that adds 40 will sometimes make the final balance different (e.g. 40) and thus violate this rule.

For every caller address, calling airDrop increases their tokenBalance by 20 (i.e., succeeds and sets balance from 0 to 20) when the caller contract/external account reports supportsToken() matching "Nu Token"; the mutant changes the supportsToken check to "My Token" causing calls from a genuine Bank implementation to revert and thus not increase balance for some caller (a contract that returns keccak256("Nu Token")).

For any caller address that implements supportsToken() returning keccak256("Nu Token"), calling airDrop from that caller always succeeds and increases its tokenBalance to 20 on the reference; the mutant requiring keccak256("My Token") will cause such a caller to fail the supportsToken check and thus not get the airdrop for some fuzzed caller address (a deployed helper), so the observable tokenBalance after calling airDrop differs.

After any single call to airDrop by any address that initially has zero balance and that is recognized by Bank as supporting the token, the reference contract always increases that caller's tokenBalance by exactly 20 (so tokenBalance == 20), whereas the buggy mutant that removed the hasNoBalance check allows repeated airDrop calls and can produce tokenBalance != 20 for some inputs (caller/address sequence).

For any address that the Bank recognizes as supporting the token, a first successful call to airDrop by that address always results in tokenBalance(address) == 20 in the reference; the mutant (which removed hasNoBalance) allows repeated successful airDrop calls and so some sequences of calls can produce tokenBalance(address) != 20.

For any address A that is recognized by Bank as supporting the token, calling airDrop exactly once from A leaves tokenBalance(A) equal to 20 and any additional immediate second call from the same address must revert or be prevented by the contract invariant — the buggy mutant allows a second call to succeed and thus can make tokenBalance(A) != 20 after two calls.
